prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks with fractional uncertainty at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Four of the six members who ranked B022 put it first, and after reading everyone's argument I still think it is the strongest entry on the list. The physics is easy to explain with a simple picture: trap many neutral atoms in a standing wave at the magic wavelength, so that the light shift is the same for both clock states and drops out, while the atoms are held tightly enough to remove Doppler and recoil effects. Katori made that idea concrete, and Ye's group then showed that the systematics can be controlled to 10^-18, including the many-body (Fermi-degenerate) clock and the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift. This is a quantitative leap in what can be measured, and the result is understood in every detail because atomic structure theory (blackbody shifts, polarizabilities, collisional shifts) can be checked against experiment. The result has been reproduced and surpassed in several independent laboratories, and clock comparisons over fibre links agree. It is a discovery about what nature allows us to see, not primarily a technological prize, even though the possible redefinition of the second is a natural later consequence. The two-name configuration is compact and fair.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the lineage of frequency combs (2005) and ion control (2012) has already been honoured, so a committee may say that this is a further refinement of precision time and frequency rather than a new phenomenon. There is also genuine credit that the two names do not cover: Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Gill, and the NIST and PTB ion and lattice efforts, and Katori's priority has to be weighed against the JILA record-setting performance. The redefinition of the second has not happened yet, so some members may reasonably want to wait for that external endorsement. Finally, as a theorist working close to this field I may rate the interpretability of clock physics higher than a colleague who values a surprise.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B022 first for a clean idea with every systematic understood, and puts B020 (Bloch, Cirac, Zoller) second, accepting that the three-person limit forces an arbitrary exclusion of Greiner and Esslinger. He also declares a closeness to circuit QED (B014) and asks others to weigh it.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and I value the declaration on B014. Where I differ is on B020. I rank it second too, but your split of Bloch with the theorists Cirac and Zoller leaves out the Mott-insulator experiment of Greiner, which I regard as the decisive demonstration. A prize that credits the proposal and the programme but not the first clear experiment would be hard to defend, so I would only support B020 with Greiner included and I would not call that settled. This is why I keep B020 as an alternative and not as part of a two-part prize. I also note that Cirac and Zoller could be recognised through other entries, which splits the theory credit.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B038 (tunnel magnetoresistance) first as an original, verified experiment with large technological consequence, and ranks B022 third, noting that the 2005 and 2012 prizes overlap with clocks and that one might wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I respect the argument for B038 as a real physical effect, and the 1995 room-temperature result by Miyazaki and Moodera is clear. My reservation is attribution and distinctness. The giant MgO result, which carries most of the technological weight, belongs partly to people outside the credited names (Yuasa and others), and the effect sits right next to the 2007 spin-valve prize, so it risks reading as a sequel. On your concern for B022, I think the overlap is smaller: combs and ion control provided tools, but the lattice clock changes the regime, because many atoms can be interrogated at once at 10^-18 with the light shift cancelled. Waiting for the redefinition would reward an administrative decision more than the physics, which is already settled.

responses.point: Danielsson also puts B022 first but ranks B028 (magic-angle graphene) third and B009 (kilonovae) fourth, and he notes that the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene is still debated and that credit between Bistritzer and MacDonald is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree that B022 is clean, and I share your reading of B028 as a real discovery that is slightly early in understanding. I would stress that the doubt about the mechanism of superconductivity matters for a committee that wants a settled interpretation, and that the experimental credit is spread over Cao, Fatemi and the group as well. On B009 you give it a higher rank than I do. I remain cautious because the evidence is essentially one event, AT2017gfo, and the gravitational-wave side was recognised in 2017, but I defer to you and to Pearce on astrophysics, and I accept that later events such as GRB 230307A strengthen the case.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B022 first and B004 (atom interferometry) second as a precision-measurement advance with real instruments, but stresses that four credited names do not fit three places and that Schmiedmayer's omission is a real allocation problem.
responses.response: I share your view that B004 speaks to the quantum-classical boundary and to precision, which is why I rank it third. But the attribution problem is worse than the Schmiedmayer question: Chu, who developed light-pulse interferometers with Kasevich, is not in the credited names and already has a prize for cooling, and Pritchard, Bordé and Kasevich each have a different claim. The fundamental-physics payoff (equivalence principle, gravitational waves) is mostly still prospective, so I find it less mature than the clocks. I would keep it as an alternative, not as a first choice.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the frequency-comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes, or as the next step in one precision-time lineage.
Fair credit to Lemonde, Gill and others not in the credited names, and the relative weights of Katori's concept and Ye's record performance.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before awarding.
My own limits on astrophysics, astroparticle and condensed-matter candidates; I defer to colleagues there and could change my second and third choices on their arguments.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B022 (Katori, Ye): my collaborations are with the Lund attosecond group (L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate) and with Keller's group at ETH, and not with the clock groups. I am a theorist in atomic, molecular and optical physics, so I am professionally close to this subfield, but this is shared closeness and not a personal tie. I do not see a recusal issue for B020, B004 or B006 either, though I note that my storage-ring recombination work is a general neighbour of precision atomic spectroscopy.
